summary: Teaches young children (roughly ages 4–6) to compare two objects directly by length or height, with endpoint alignment as the explicit heart of the skill: line up one end at a common starting line, THEN compare the far ends. Addresses the classic errors of judging by whichever end 'sticks out farthest', ignoring a raised baseline for height, and non-conservation (believing length changes when an object is bent or rotated). Builds precise comparative language (longer/shorter, taller/shorter) rather than the global 'bigger'.
misconceptions: Judging by one endpoint — picks the object that 'sticks out farthest' at one end without aligning the starting ends
Ignoring the baseline for height — calls the tower whose top is higher 'taller' even though it stands on a book and has fewer blocks
Non-conservation — believes an object becomes longer when turned vertical, or that a ribbon becomes shorter when curved because its endpoints move closer
Using undifferentiated 'bigger' instead of the specific comparative word (longer/taller), signalling the length attribute is not yet differentiated

activities.title: Line up the ends, then compare (ribbons)
steps: Look at two ribbons lying staggered on the table, with the SHORTER ribbon shifted so its right end pokes out past the longer ribbon's right end and the near ends left unaligned
Say which ribbon is longer and explain how you know
Either slide both ribbons to a common starting line, or (in a non-draggable image) draw a line to mark the common start, then compare the far ends again
Meet a 'mixed-up' puppet (e.g. Mr MixUp) who compares WITHOUT lining up the starting ends; catch and fix the puppet's mistake
Answer: 'Where does each ribbon START? Put your finger on the beginning of each one.'
activities.insight: To compare fairly, line up one end of each object at a common start; then the far ends show which is longer. Looking at the far ends tells you nothing reliable while the starting ends are not matched. The object that 'sticks out' at one end is not automatically the longer one.

activities.title: Compare towers from a common base
steps: Look at two towers built from identical blocks: a taller tower (more blocks) standing on the floor, and a shorter tower (fewer blocks) standing on a thick book so its TOP is higher
Say which tower is taller and explain how you know
Bring the book-raised tower down onto the floor (or reason explicitly about the book's height) so both start from the same surface, then compare again
Try a harder case: raise the shorter tower even higher on two books — 'now is it taller? What if I put it on the floor?'
activities.insight: To compare heights fairly, both objects must start from a common base; you cannot judge just by where the tops are. Here the shorter tower looks taller only because it sits on a book; move both to the same surface to compare fairly.

activities.title: Does length change when you bend it? (conservation)
steps: Look at two ribbons of exactly equal length; one is then bent into a wavy curve
Predict: 'are they still the same length, or is one longer now?'
Watch (or press 'straighten') as the curved ribbon is straightened back out, and check the prediction
Try the rotate version: an equal stick turned vertical — predict whether it 'got longer', then restore it to compare
activities.insight: Length does not change just because an object is bent or turned — a bent ribbon is the same length when straightened; a stick is the same length lying down or standing up (though how tall it stands does depend on which way it is turned).

activities.title: Say it precisely: longer, shorter, taller
steps: After each comparison, describe the result with the specific comparative word — 'this ribbon is LONGER', 'this tower is TALLER' — not just 'bigger'
Match the word to the attribute: longer/shorter for length laid out, taller/shorter for height standing up
Describe practical real-object pairs (two pencils, two strips) using long/short, longer/shorter, tall/short
activities.insight: Length and height are specific attributes with specific words; naming them precisely shows you are comparing the right thing, not just overall 'size'.

checkQuestion: Set three tasks and WATCH — do not explain the method first. (1) Lay two ribbons of different lengths on the table STAGGERED: shift the SHORTER ribbon forward so its far end sticks out past the longer one's far end, and leave the near ends unaligned. Ask 'which ribbon is longer? Show me how you know.' (2) Build two block towers — one taller tower on the floor, and a shorter tower standing on a thick book so its TOP is higher. Ask 'which tower is taller?' (3) Take two ribbons of exactly equal length; bend one into a wavy curve. Ask 'are they still the same length, or is one longer now?' Watch whether the child aligns the starting ends, accounts for the raised base, and conserves length.
checkAnswer: (1) Lines up one end of both ribbons at a common starting line, then compares the far ends, and names the genuinely longer ribbon (not the one that was poking out). (2) Compares from a common base — recognises the book-raised tower only looks taller, brings both to the same surface or reasons about the book's height, and identifies the tower with more actual height. (3) Says the two ribbons are still the same length even though one is now curved — length is conserved when a ribbon is bent.
